"""Praise-and-excellence detector for layer 15's MLP hidden unit 320 (down_proj component 320).

This component is almost exactly one hidden unit of the layer-15 MLP: its input direction
is the unit's own basis vector, and its output direction is the unit's down-projection row
scaled by about 1.85. So its activation is that unit's value, which goes strongly negative
on words of praise and excellence ("unparalleled", "breakthrough", "legendary", "renowned",
"excellent") and on the words that set one up ("world", "top", "best", "industry",
"leading", "great"). It is near zero, and mildly positive, elsewhere.

Logit lens: its output direction, read backwards, promotes words like "-notch", "-worthy",
"excellence", "caliber", "-tier" when the activation is negative, so the unit helps the
model predict an acclaim word next.

This program is a word lookup: a strong negative value on acclaim words, a weaker negative
value on words that usually lead into one, and 0 everywhere else. It sees only the current
token. It explains only a small share of the variance: the component's sign and its broad
theme are right, but most of its variance comes from context this list cannot see.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Words that name excellence, acclaim or a standout quality (the unit's strongest negatives).
ACCLAIM = frozenset(
    """unparalleled breakthrough landmark excellence excellent excellently legendary memorable
    exceptional exceptionally renowned stunning superb pioneering pioneer revolutionary
    spectacular extraordinary extraordinarily incredible fantastic amazing remarkable iconic
    outstanding awesome brilliant unmatched impressive masterpiece genius elite finest
    unforgettable -leading -winning -class -quality -notch -worthy -tier -grade
    业界 领军 领先 经典 一流 同类 极品 卓越 杰出 优秀 顶尖 巅峰 精品 赞誉 惊艳""".split()
)

# Words that usually lead into a superlative or a praise phrase ("the world's best", "top quality").
SETUP = frozenset(
    """great best top world industry leading leader leaders high highest most very extremely
    unique premier classic famous superior wonderful stellar ultra super highly truly first
    世界 全国 第一 超 最 最佳 最好 精英 巨星 好评""".split()
)

ACCLAIM_VALUE = -3.0
SETUP_VALUE = -1.0


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    """Activation at this position: negative on praise words, weaker on words that set one up."""
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    if word in ACCLAIM:
        return carry, ACCLAIM_VALUE
    if word in SETUP:
        return carry, SETUP_VALUE
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 321.

What it does, in plain terms: most of the time this component is small, diffuse noise.
Its clearest response is to correlative pairs. Its activation tends to be positive on the
first word of a "between X and Y", "both X and Y", "either X or Y" (and "entre X y",
"zwischen X und", "между X и"). It stays mildly positive on the words that follow such an
opener while the pair is still open, i.e. until an "and"/"or" or a sentence break closes it.

The rule: a word right after an opener gets the first-item value; a word later in an open
pair gets a smaller value; everything else gets 0. The values are the group means measured
on training text (about 0.9 and 0.4). Positives are about two in three, so this is a bet
that is right on average, not on each token.

What the rule leaves out: the large negative activations sit inside parallel or list
constructions ("life or death", "good and evil", "tragic, vibrant") and have no simple
concept behind them, and most of the variance is diffuse token-level noise. So the rule
explains only about 1% of the variance.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Words that open a two-part pair: "between A and B", "both A and B", "either A or B".
PAIR_OPENERS = {"between", "both", "either", "entre", "zwischen", "между"}
# Words that close a pair; a sentence break also closes it.
PAIR_CLOSERS = {"and", "or", ".", "\n"}

FIRST_ITEM = 0.9   # the word right after the opener
OPEN_PAIR = 0.4    # later words while the pair is still open
WINDOW = 8         # how far back to look for an opener


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    t = prefix.position
    doc = prefix.document_ids[t]
    # Words before this token in the same document, nearest first.
    recent = []
    for k in range(t - 1, max(-1, t - WINDOW - 1), -1):
        if prefix.document_ids[k] != doc:
            break
        recent.append(prefix.token_strings[k].strip().lower())

    if recent and recent[0] in PAIR_OPENERS:
        return carry, FIRST_ITEM
    for word in recent:
        if word in PAIR_CLOSERS:
            break
        if word in PAIR_OPENERS:
            return carry, OPEN_PAIR
    return carry, 0.0

"""Predicts the component's activation from the kind of the current token.

The component (layer 15, MLP down-projection unit 322) has a small, diffuse
activation: mean 0.03, spread about 0.34 either side. Its sign and size depend
on the wider context, which a token-only program cannot see, so most of the
variance is out of reach. The best token-level guess is a small offset by the
kind of token just read: function words, punctuation, word pieces, digits.
"""
import re

READS = ()

FUNCTION_WORDS = frozenset(
    "of the a an and or to in on at by for with from as is was be are were "
    "that this it its which who not but if so than then there these those "
    "he she they we you i his her their".split()
)

# Mean activation of each kind of token, measured on 40,000 training rows.
KIND_MEAN = {
    "space": 0.006,
    "digit": 0.0,
    "capitalized word": 0.012,
    "function word": 0.017,
    "word": 0.02,
    "punctuation": 0.024,
    "word piece": 0.039,
    "other": 0.03,
}


def kind(text):
    core = text.strip()
    if not core:
        return "space"
    if re.fullmatch(r"\d+", core):
        return "digit"
    if re.fullmatch(r"[^\w\s]+", core):
        return "punctuation"
    if text[:1] == " " and core.lower() in FUNCTION_WORDS:
        return "function word"
    if text[:1] == " " and core[:1].isupper():
        return "capitalized word"
    if text[:1] == " ":
        return "word"
    if core.isalpha():
        return "word piece"
    return "other"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return carry, KIND_MEAN[kind(prefix.token_strings[-1])]

"""Layer 15 MLP down-projection component 324: chat-turn "user" markers and shell pipes.

Two things make this component fire, both on the token where a new piece of
structure begins:

1. The role word "user" that opens a user turn after an assistant turn
   ("...<|im_end|>\\n<|im_start|>user"). This is its strongest response.
2. A pipe "|" inside a shell command line (for example "... 2>&1 | tail" or
   "grep ... | head"), where the pipe starts a second command.

Everywhere else it sits near its small typical value.
"""

import re

READS = ()

TYPICAL = -0.035  # the component's mean activation on ordinary tokens
TURN_START = 3.7  # "user" after "<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>"
DOC_START = 0.6  # "user" right after "<|im_start|>" at a document start
PIPE = 2.9  # a "|" on a line that looks like a shell command
SHELL = re.compile(
    r"\b(grep|head|tail|cat|ls|sort|wc|xargs|find|echo|sed|awk|npm|git|python|node|pytest|make)\b|2>|&1"
)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    s = prefix.token_strings
    if s[-1].strip() == "|":
        line = []
        for tok in reversed(s[:-1][-40:]):
            if "\n" in tok:
                break
            line.append(tok)
        if SHELL.search("".join(reversed(line))):
            return carry, PIPE
        return carry, TYPICAL
    if len(s) < 2 or s[-1] != "user" or s[-2] != "<|im_start|>":
        return carry, TYPICAL
    if len(s) >= 4 and s[-3] == "\n" and s[-4] == "<|im_end|>":
        return carry, TURN_START
    return carry, DOC_START

"""Link-introducing punctuation, as a rule (layer 15 MLP, component 325).

This component goes negative where the text is about to point the reader to a web
address or a reference, and it is most negative on the words and marks that lead into
one: "see", "https", "www", "://", and the colon or bracket that opens a link or a
source ("Read more:", "More information:", "available at:", "Docs (", "Source: ...").
Ordinary prose punctuation after a word is mildly negative; code-style tokens and most
words are near zero. The rule gives each token a value from its kind:

  - link words and URL pieces (see, https, http, www, ://)            -> -2.7
  - a colon that ends a label or introduces a value (":", " :", "：",
    "):", "}:", ...)                                                    -> -2.8
  - a space-led opening bracket or parenthesis (" (", " [", " （")      -> -2.0
  - a space-led dash or arrow, a semicolon (" —", " –", " ->", " |", ";") -> -1.2
  - a JSON-style key colon ('":')                                       -> -1.0
  - " by" and " from"                                                   -> -0.4
  - anything else (including "::" and unspaced "(" or "[")              -> 0

It reads only the current token, so it needs no memory of the text before it.
What this simple version gets: about 0.14 of the variance of the component's
activations on the eval rows (r = 0.38). The rest is spread over many tokens: a
token-by-token lookup of the component's mean would reach about 0.18 on training text,
and that table would add only a few hundredths. The component's positive values in
code and markup (for example "</tool_call>", "path", "style") are not modelled.
"""

READS = ()

LINK_WORDS = {"see", "See", "https", "http", "www"}
PROSE_BRACKETS = {" (", " [", " （"}
DASHES = {" —", " –", " ->", " ⇒", " |", " →", ";", "；"}
WEAK_WORDS = {" by", " from"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    raw = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    word = raw.strip()
    if word in LINK_WORDS or "://" in raw:
        value = -2.7
    elif raw.rstrip("\n").endswith((":", "：")) and word not in ("::", '":'):
        value = -2.8
    elif raw == '":':
        value = -1.0
    elif raw in PROSE_BRACKETS:
        value = -2.0
    elif raw in DASHES:
        value = -1.2
    elif raw in WEAK_WORDS:
        value = -0.4
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, value

"""Layer 15, MLP down-projection, component 326.

What it responds to (measured on training text; the activation is mostly small noise,
with rare large values):
- Positive inside conversion wording: the few tokens after "convert", "conversion",
  "converting" or "converter", above all a unit or measure being converted
  ("convert inches to feet", "ml", "kilograms", "tsp"). Its write direction promotes
  "to" / "into", the word that follows such a phrase.
- Negative on words that name a starting point or an alternative: "from", "than",
  "instead", "replace(d)", "versus", "rather", "between", "not". Its write direction
  suppresses "to" / "into" there.
- Near zero everywhere else.

It predicts one mean per group, so it is a coarse description: it captures only a
small part of the variance.
"""

READS = ()

CONVERT_WORDS = ("convert", "conversion", "converting", "converter")
CONTRAST_WORDS = {"from", "than", "instead", "replace", "replaced", "replacing",
                  "versus", "vs", "rather", "between", "not"}
UNITS = {"kilogram", "kilograms", "gram", "grams", "kg", "mg", "meter", "meters", "metre",
         "cm", "mm", "km", "inch", "inches", "foot", "feet", "ft", "yard", "mile", "miles",
         "ounce", "ounces", "pound", "pounds", "lb", "lbs", "ton", "tons", "gallon",
         "gallons", "cup", "cups", "tablespoon", "tablespoons", "tsp", "tbsp", "ml", "l",
         "liter", "liters", "litre", "mole", "moles", "radian", "radians", "degree",
         "degrees", "second", "seconds", "bit", "bits", "byte", "bytes", "hex", "binary",
         "decimal", "fraction", "³", "/cm", "/m", "wt", "utc"}
CONVERT_VALUE = 0.6      # mean activation on other tokens in conversion wording
UNIT_CONVERT_VALUE = 4.6 # mean activation on a unit inside conversion wording
CONTRAST_VALUE = -0.28   # mean activation on starting-point / alternative words
WINDOW = 3               # tokens after a conversion word that still count


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    strings = prefix.token_strings
    t = prefix.position
    cur = strings[t].strip().lower()
    if cur in CONTRAST_WORDS:
        return carry, CONTRAST_VALUE
    for back in range(WINDOW + 1):
        j = t - back
        if j < 0 or ids[j] != ids[t]:
            break
        if strings[j].strip().lower().startswith(CONVERT_WORDS):
            return carry, UNIT_CONVERT_VALUE if cur in UNITS else CONVERT_VALUE
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 327: a "coordinated predicate verb" detector.

Positive where the token is the verb or auxiliary that opens a predicate right after a
coordinating conjunction (and / but / or / nor / yet), i.e. a verb whose subject is
not repeated: "... was tired, and [was] ...", "but [will] ...". Auxiliaries and modals
there give the largest values; other verbs a smaller one.

Negative where the token is a transitional word opening a sentence ("Also,",
"Moreover,", "However,", "Actually,", "Wait", "And", "But" at a sentence start).

Everything else is predicted as 0. The rest of the component's variance is diffuse and
is not captured by this program.
"""

import wordnet

READS = ()

COORDINATORS = {"and", "but", "or", "nor", "yet"}
AUXILIARIES = set(
    "is are was were be been being am has have had do does did "
    "will would can could may might must shall should".split()
)
OPENERS = set(
    "also moreover furthermore however actually finally indeed alternatively "
    "additionally likewise anyway fortunately interestingly meanwhile lastly "
    "besides plus still now well yet and but wait".split()
)
SENTENCE_END = set(".!?。！？\n\"”")


def _word(text):
    return text.strip().lower()


def _starts_sentence(prev_text):
    return prev_text is None or prev_text.strip() == "" or prev_text[-1] in SENTENCE_END


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if same_doc else None
    word = _word(prefix.token_strings[-1])
    if prev is not None and _word(prev) in COORDINATORS:
        if word in AUXILIARIES:
            return carry, 7.0
        if word.isalpha() and "verb" in wordnet.parts_of_speech(word):
            return carry, 2.5
    if word in OPENERS and (word == "wait" or _starts_sentence(prev)):
        return carry, -2.5
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 328: a diffuse feature with no simple surface rule.

What is known about it:
- Its activation is (MLP hidden unit input x @ V_c) * ||U_c||. Across 2M training
  tokens it has mean ~0.04 and std ~0.35, both signs, and is spread over many tokens
  rather than firing on a few. It is ~0 at a document's first token.
- About 36% of its variance is the single MLP hidden unit 328 of layer 15 (its
  correlation with that unit is 0.55). The rest is spread over thousands of units.
- Nothing in the prefix explains it: the current token's identity, the previous token,
  token class (punctuation, digits, leading space, script), the position in the document,
  whether the token repeated earlier, and the document's identity each explain under 2%
  of its variance on held-out rows. Its sign does not track the model's own probability
  of concessive words ("despite", "although", ...), though its output direction's logit
  lens points that way.

So this program predicts the component's mean activation at every position. That
explains none of its variance (R^2 about 0), and it is the honest readable version:
no short rule here captures what the unit responds to.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.0365
"""The component's mean activation over the eval rows."""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Predict the mean activation at every position; no state is carried."""
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # A person can check the constant against the stored activations: its variance explained
    # is 1 - sum((t - p)^2) / sum((t - mean t)^2), which is about 0 for this constant.
    print("predicts", MEAN_ACTIVATION, "everywhere")

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 329: predict its typical activation.

This component is effectively inert: its causal importance is ~0 at every token,
and switching it off barely changes the model's next-token predictions. Its
activation is a small, diffuse signal (std ~0.28, mean ~0.04) that does not track
any token identity, token class, or position we could find. So the honest
readable prediction is its mean activation, a constant.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.04


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Ranking-context guess for layers.15.mlp.down_proj:330 (L15 MLP down_proj, component 330).

What the component does: its activation is usually small (median ~0.02) with rare
large spikes, mostly negative, that write a "ranking / contender / beat" direction
into the residual stream (its output, read through the unembedding, promotes words
like "ranked", "contenders", "leaderboard", "rank"). The large spikes, of both signs,
occur in passages about sports, standings, records and comparisons ("moved up from
fifth position", "trailing just", "followed by", "the first").

What this program does: it only encodes that context. It predicts a small value
(0.02) on a token when one of the last 10 tokens of the same document is a ranking
or competition word, and 0 otherwise. Its sign and size within those passages are
NOT predictable from the prefix, so this captures almost none of the variance.
"""

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

RANKING_WORDS = frozenset(
    """rank ranked ranking rankings ranks contender contenders leader leaders
    winner winners win wins won beat beats record records champion champions
    first second third fourth fifth top position positions best title titles
    trailing lead leads season league tournament team teams match game games
    player players score goal goals final finals cup qualify qualified
    than among highest largest most followed ahead behind""".split()
)
WINDOW = 10
IN_CONTEXT = 0.02


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    recent = carry or []
    if len(prefix.token_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        recent = []
    value = IN_CONTEXT if any(recent) else 0.0
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    recent = (recent + [word in RANKING_WORDS])[-WINDOW:]
    return recent, value

"""Null program for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 331.

This component is layer 15's MLP hidden unit 331, read through its down projection (its
V vector is 66% that unit). Its activation is sparse and heavy-tailed: mean 0.03, std 0.48,
with the largest values on about 0.3% of positions, of both signs.

We looked for a readable predictor and found none: the current token, the previous or
next token, whether the token repeats earlier in the document, coarse token classes
(digits, spaces, CJK, code punctuation, ...) and document identity each explain roughly
zero variance out of sample. So this program predicts 0 everywhere, the same as
switching the unit off.
"""

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # No readable feature predicts the activation, so the best readable guess is zero.
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP unit 332's down_proj component: a weak negation signal.

The component reads one MLP hidden unit (index 332 of layer 15) and writes it into the
residual stream with a scale of about 0.26. Its activation is noise-like overall: mean 0.03,
std 0.39, and it does not follow token identity, token class or short context, which
together explain about 1% of its variance. The one readable tendency is that negation words
push it up: "not" averages 0.22, "never" and "ever" about 0.18, "no" 0.10, against a baseline
of 0.025. Those words are rare, so this rule explains well under 1% of the variance.

This program predicts the negation level for negation words and the baseline everywhere else.
"""

READS = ()

BASELINE = 0.025
NEGATION_WORDS = {"not", "no", "never", "ever", "nor", "neither", "without", "cannot", "none", "nothing", "nobody", "n't"}
NEGATION_LEVEL = 0.2


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    return carry, NEGATION_LEVEL if word in NEGATION_WORDS else BASELINE

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:333 fires on the word "or" (and its
translations) when it joins two alternatives: "get the money or pay the",
"cap ... lace front or monofilament top", "comando ou terminal", "Obst oder Gemüse".

It is a disjunction detector. On the token that says "or" it predicts a
strength (about 4 for the plain English "or", about the same for "ou", "oder",
"или", "或"; weaker for "Or", "nor", "else", and the ambiguous Spanish/Italian
"o"). On every other token it predicts 0. The large negative dips of the
component are not captured here: they are diffuse and not tied to any word.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Strength on the token that says "or" between alternatives, by word.
OR_WORDS = {
    " or": 4.0,  # English "X or Y"
    " ou": 4.0,  # Portuguese / French
    " oder": 4.0,  # German
    " или": 5.0,  # Russian
    "或": 3.0,  # Chinese
    " tai": 3.0,  # Finnish
    " eller": 3.5,  # Scandinavian
    "_or": 3.0,  # "or" inside an identifier, e.g. name_or_id
    " Or": 1.8,  # sentence-initial "Or"
    "Or": 1.4,
    "or": 0.7,  # "or" without a leading space, e.g. after "("
    "/or": 1.2,
    " nor": 1.5,
    " o": 1.2,  # Spanish / Italian "o" (also a Portuguese article)
    " else": 0.9,
    " Alternatively": 1.3,
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    """Activation at this position: the disjunction strength of the newest token."""
    return carry, OR_WORDS.get(prefix.token_strings[-1], 0.0)

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 334: a dense, context-dependent readout that no simple
concept I tested explains, so this program predicts its mean value at every position.

What was checked on 4096 training rows (2M tokens): the activation is symmetric around 0
(mean 0.02, std 0.70). Token identity, character class (digit, CJK, punctuation, newline,
...), previous-token class, position in the row or document, repeated tokens and bigrams,
and the model's own entropy and next-token surprisal each explain almost none of it
(R^2 below 0.002). A linear probe on the MLP input reaches R^2 about 0.19, but only as a
dense direction with no human-readable meaning. The component almost never passes the
causal-importance threshold (about 6e-5 of tokens), and switching it off barely changes the
model's next-token distribution.

The program therefore predicts the constant 0.02 (the mean) everywhere.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.02


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 336: a pronoun component.

In plain terms: this component goes negative on personal pronouns, and the
size of the dip depends on which pronoun it is. The strongest dips are on
first-person plural and "you"-type words (our, we, 我, 我们, my, your, you).
Subject and possessive pronouns (I, he, she, they, their, his, its, 他, 她, 你)
dip less, and object pronouns (him, them, us, her, me) hardly at all. On every
other token the component sits near its average, a small positive value. Most of
its variance is spread over ordinary tokens, which this program does not capture.

The program is a lookup of three word classes with one value each.
"""

READS = ()

# Lower-cased pronoun tokens, grouped by how strongly the component dips on them.
STRONG = {"our", "we", "you", "your", "my", "我", "我们", "我的", "你"}
MEDIUM = {"i", "he", "she", "they", "their", "his", "its", "他", "她", "您"}
WEAK = {"him", "them", "us", "her", "me"}

AVERAGE = 0.09  # the component's average value on ordinary tokens
STRONG_VALUE = -1.2  # average value on the strong group
MEDIUM_VALUE = -0.7  # average value on the medium group
WEAK_VALUE = -0.2  # average value on the weak group


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    if word in STRONG:
        return carry, STRONG_VALUE
    if word in MEDIUM:
        return carry, MEDIUM_VALUE
    if word in WEAK:
        return carry, WEAK_VALUE
    return carry, AVERAGE

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 337, read out through one down-projection direction.

What it responds to, as far as word lists can show. Its activation is mostly small
(std 0.36) and depends on context that no word list captures: a lexical lookup of the
current token explains about 3% of its variance, and a neighbourhood-of-words linear
model about 2%. The parts with a consistent sign are:
- Place and nationality names (Australia, Kansas, American, Nigeria): clearly negative.
- Scope words about the whole world or many countries (world, global, countries,
  Europe, US): negative, more so than place names.
- Birth words (birth, born) and politician/official nouns: positive.
Everywhere else the activation sits near its mean, about -0.02.

The program reads the current token alone and predicts one of these four values.
"""

import pycountry
import regex
import wordnet

READS = ()

US_STATES = {s.name for s in pycountry.subdivisions.get(country_code="US")}
COUNTRIES = {c.name for c in pycountry.countries}
SCOPE_WORDS = {
    "world", "worldwide", "global", "globally", "international", "countries",
    "country", "nation", "nations", "national", "nationwide", "US", "USA", "UK",
    "EU", "America", "Europe", "Asia", "Africa",
}
BIRTH_WORDS = {"birth", "births", "born", "birthday"}
OFFICIAL_WORDS = {"politician", "politicians", "mayor", "officials", "coaches"}
NAME = regex.compile(r"\p{Lu}[\p{L}'-]*")

PLACE_VALUE = -0.13
SCOPE_VALUE = -0.35
BIRTH_OFFICIAL_VALUE = 0.25
OTHER_VALUE = -0.02


def is_place_or_nationality(word):

# "" marks the start of a document or a line break.

    "", ".", "!", "?", "on", "by", "for", "of", "with", "from", "in", "at", "to", "after",
    "about", "under", "over", "during", "into", "through", "since", "until", "before", "like",
    "than",
}

# WordNet lexicographer classes of nouns, by how strongly they follow a demonstrative.
ABSTRACT = {
    "noun.act", "noun.attribute", "noun.cognition", "noun.communication", "noun.event",
    "noun.feeling", "noun.phenomenon", "noun.possession", "noun.process", "noun.relation",
    "noun.state", "noun.Tops",
}
THINGS = {
    "noun.animal", "noun.artifact", "noun.body", "noun.food", "noun.object", "noun.person",
    "noun.plant", "noun.substance",
}
TIME_PLACE = {"noun.group", "noun.location", "noun.quantity", "noun.shape", "noun.time"}

SCALE = -11.0


def _back(prefix, k):
    """The stripped, lowercased token k places before the newest, or "" at a document's start."""
    i = len(prefix.token_strings) - 1 - k
    if i < 0 or prefix.document_ids[i] != prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        return ""
    return prefix.token_strings[i].strip().lower()


def _is_word(text):
    """A word: letters only, and not a short English fragment (CJK words are kept)."""
    return text.isalpha() and (len(text) >= 3 or not text.isascii())


@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def _noun_kind(word):
    """How strongly a word after a demonstrative responds, by its WordNet classes."""
    classes = set(wordnet.categories(word)) if wordnet.parts_of_speech(word) else set()
    if classes & ABSTRACT:
        return 1.0
    if classes & THINGS:
        return 0.85
    if classes & TIME_PLACE:
        return 0.35
    if any(c.startswith("noun") for c in classes):

    return 0.25

    if weight == 0.0 or not _is_word(word):

    return carry, SCALE * weight * _noun_kind(word)

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:355: a weak 'number in ordinary text' feature.

What it responds to. The component is negative on number tokens and near zero
elsewhere:
- Digit tokens are negative on average (about -1). The second digit of a number
  is the most negative (about -1.7 on average); the first and later digits are
  about -0.8.
- English number words (' five', ' seventeen', ' third', ' half') are negative,
  about -1.7 on average.
- Digits are less negative in code-like text. The program measures this as the
  share of code-like tokens (brackets, operators, '=', '_', slashes) since the
  start of the document, and treats it as a rough proxy for code versus prose.
- Digits are a little less negative further into a document.

Everything else is predicted as 0. The program keeps per-document counters in
its carry, so it resets at each document boundary.

This is a rough, token-level description. It explains about 10% of the variance
of the activation. The rest sits in context the program cannot see (its size
varies strongly from one document to the next, and a single number's
activation can reach -39 or +14), so it is not a full account of the component.
"""
import math
import re

READS = ()

NUMBER_WORDS = frozenset(
    "zero one two three four five six seven eight nine ten eleven twelve thirteen "
    "fourteen fifteen sixteen seventeen eighteen nineteen twenty thirty forty fifty "
    "sixty seventy eighty ninety hundred thousand million billion first second third "
    "fourth fifth sixth seventh eighth ninth tenth half".split()
)
CODE_LIKE = re.compile(r"[{}()\[\];=<>_\\/]")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (document id, tokens so far in the document, code-like tokens so far,
    #         length of the digit run ending at the previous token)
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        carry = (doc, 0, 0, 0)
    _, n, code, run = carry
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    n += 1
    code += 1 if CODE_LIKE.search(tok) else 0
    is_digit = len(tok) == 1 and tok.isdigit()
    run = run + 1 if is_digit else 0
    carry = (doc, n, code, run)

    if is_digit:
        share = code / n  # share of code-like tokens in this document so far
        offset = {1: -0.5, 2: -1.3}.get(run, -0.3)  # position within the number
        return carry, -2.0 + 3.8 * share + 0.26 * math.log(n) + offset
    if tok.strip().lower() in NUMBER_WORDS:
        return carry, -1.7
    return carry, 0.0

"hypothetical / imagined framing" feature. Its activation is mostly small and noisy, and most
of the variance is context the current token does not show; the part a word list can read is
that it is large on wish, imagine, hypothetical and theory words, moderate on ideal, potential,
hope and dream words, and weakly positive on modal and conditional words (would, could, if).

Everything else is predicted as 0.

    r"speculat|hoped$|envision|dreamed$|fantas|w(ä|a)re$|h(ä|a)tte$)"

MEDIUM = re.compile(
    r"^(ideal|potential|possibilit|aspiration|conceivable|pretend|hope|dream|deserv|desire|"
    r"ought|w(ü|u)rde$|k(ö|o)nnte$|m(ö|o)chte$|simulat|scenario|imagin|supposed|assuming)"
)

of a UTF-8 character (U+FFFD) is strongly negative. Punctuation, digits and spaces are
slightly negative.

from functools import lru_cache

    (True, False): -1.30,
    (False, True): -1.03,
    (True, True): -3.28,
}


@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def frequency(word):
    """How common the letters are as a word, in its most common language (Zipf scale)."""
    return max(zipf_frequency(word.lower(), lang) for lang in LANGS)

"""Seams between declarations in source code (layers.15.mlp.down_proj, component 375).

This component is quiet on most text and turns on inside source code, most of all at the
seam between two members of a program: a function or method has just closed (a `}` was the
last non-blank token) and the next declaration is about to start. Its strongest firings sit
on the indentation or blank line after such a `}`, and on declaration keywords themselves
(`def`, `func`, `void`, `public`, `static`, `#[`, `/**`).

The program reads only the prefix and keeps two facts about it:
  - the newest token's class: a declaration keyword, a token with a closing brace, an
    indentation or blank-line token, or anything else;
  - whether the last non-blank token closed a block, and whether the recent text looks like
    code (at least 30% of the last 32 tokens hold code marks or start a line with indentation).

A class sets a base value, higher in code than in prose; a block that just closed multiplies
it by 4. Everything else predicts 0. The values are the class means measured on training text.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

DECLARATIONS = frozenset(
    {"def", "func", "function", "fn", "pub", "public", "private", "protected", "static",
     "void", "class", "struct", "impl", "override", "export", "#[", "/**", "@"}
)
CODE_MARKS = frozenset("{};()=<>[]")
WINDOW = 32
CODE_SHARE = 0.3
AFTER_CLOSE = 4.0

# class: (value in prose, value in code)
BASE = {
    "declaration": (0.4, 1.2),
    "closing_brace": (0.14, 0.6),
    "indent_or_blank": (0.0, 0.13),
}


def _code_like(text: str) -> bool:
    return any(ch in CODE_MARKS for ch in text) or text.startswith(("\n", "\t", "  "))


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    new_doc = (
        carry is None
        or len(prefix.token_ids) == 1
        or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    )
    after_close, flags = (False, []) if new_doc else carry
    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    flags = (flags + [int(_code_like(text))])[-WINDOW:]
    in_code = sum(flags) / len(flags) >= CODE_SHARE

    stripped = text.strip()
    if not stripped:
        kind = "indent_or_blank"
    elif stripped in DECLARATIONS:
        kind = "declaration"
    elif "}" in text:
        kind = "closing_brace"
    else:
        kind = None

    value = 0.0
    if kind is not None:
        prose, code = BASE[kind]
        value = code if in_code else prose
        if after_close:
            value *= AFTER_CLOSE
    next_after_close = after_close if not stripped else "}" in text
    return (next_after_close, flags), float(value)

"""Layer-15 MLP component 381 (down_proj), read as a "noun inside a modified noun phrase" detector.

The component is negative on nouns, and most negative on a noun that follows another content
word, an adjective or a noun, as in "other engineering components" or "popular mapping applications".
A plural noun is more negative than a singular one, and a noun that is not an everyday word
("structures", "processes", "facilities") is more negative than a common one ("time", "day",
"way"). A singular noun right after a function word ("the", "a", "of", "in") is near zero.
Verbs, adjectives and function words are small. Past-tense verbs are weakly positive, which
this program leaves out.

The program looks only at the current word and the word before it. Part of speech comes from
WordNet, plural from inflect, and how common a word is from wordfreq. The numbers are rounded
least-squares fits to the component's activations on training text.

import wordfreq
import wordnet

_ENGINE = inflect.engine()

# Closed-class words: articles, determiners, prepositions, auxiliaries, pronouns, conjunctions.
# WordNet tags some of them as nouns or adjectives ("a", "no", "in"), so they are excluded.
_FUNCTION_WORDS = set(
    """a an the this that these those each every either neither some any no all both several
    many few more most much other another such same own first second last new your my his her
    its our their whose which what of in on at by for with from to into onto over under about
    above below through during before after between among against within without across along
    around behind beyond near upon as than like via per is are was were be been being am do
    does did done have has had having will would shall should can could may might must it he
    she we they you i me him us them one two three there here when where why how if so but
    and or nor yet because while not only also just very too even still then once again""".split()
)


def _word(text):
    """The lowercase word a token spells, if it begins a word (leading space), else None."""
    if not text.startswith(" "):
        return None
    word = text.strip().lower()
    return word if word.isalpha() else None


def _is_noun(word):
    return "noun" in wordnet.parts_of_speech(word)


def _is_plural_noun(word):
    return _is_noun(word) and word.endswith("s") and bool(_ENGINE.singular_noun(word))


def _modifier_kind(word):
    """'noun' or 'adjective' if the word can modify a noun (and is not a function word), else None."""
    if word is None or word in _FUNCTION_WORDS:
        return None
    pos = wordnet.parts_of_speech(word)
    if "noun" in pos:
        return "noun"
    return "adjective" if "adjective" in pos else None


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = _word(prefix.token_strings[-1])
    if word is None or word in _FUNCTION_WORDS or not _is_noun(word):
        return carry, -0.05

    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    before = _word(prefix.token_strings[-2]) if same_doc else None
    modifier = _modifier_kind(before)

    plural = _is_plural_noun(word)
    specialised = 2.5 <= wordfreq.zipf_frequency(word, "en") < 5.5

    value = 0.2
    if plural:
        value -= 0.5
    if specialised:
        value -= 0.4
    if modifier == "adjective":
        value -= 2.4 + (0.9 if plural else 0.0)
    elif modifier == "noun":
        value -= 1.5 + (0.5 if plural else 0.0)
    return carry, float(value)
